description: This section of Logical Reasoning is based on calculating time and dates. It includes concepts related to the angle between clock hands, odd days, and finding the day of the week for specific dates.

sections.title: Clocks - Basic Concepts
sections.description: Basic understanding of the speed of clock hands and the angle between them.

key_concepts.explanation: The minute hand covers a distance of 6° in 1 minute (6° per minute).
The hour hand covers a distance of 1/2° in 1 minute (1/2° per minute).
When both hands move in the same direction, their relative speed is 5.5° per minute.

sections.title: Calendars - Basic Rules
sections.description: Fundamental principles of calendars related to identifying odd days and leap years.

key_concepts.explanation: The remainder left after dividing the total number of days by 7 is called odd days.
It has 365 days. Dividing 365 by 7 gives a remainder of 1, hence 1 odd day.
It has 366 days. It is perfectly divisible by 4 and contains 2 odd days.
Years ending in '00'. A century year is a leap year only if it is divisible by 400 (e.g., 1600, 2000).

sections.title: Calendars - Finding Day of the Week
sections.description: Step-by-step process to find the day of the week for any given historical or future date.

steps.title: Century Odd Days
steps.detail: Find the odd days of the century immediately preceding the given year (100 years = 5, 200 years = 3, 300 years = 1, 400 years = 0).

steps.title: Odd Days of Remaining Years
steps.detail: Count the number of leap years and ordinary years in the completed years after the century and before the current year to calculate their odd days.

steps.title: Odd Days of Current Year
steps.detail: Calculate total odd days starting from January to the given date (e.g., 3 for Jan, 0 or 1 for Feb).

steps.title: Final Calculation and Code Matching
steps.detail: Add all odd days and divide by 7. Match the final remainder with the day code (0=Sunday, 1=Monday, 2=Tuesday, 3=Wednesday, 4=Thursday, 5=Friday, 6=Saturday).

sections.title: Calendars - Repetition of Year
sections.description: Rules to identify future or past years that share the exact same calendar.

results: The calendar of a leap year repeats after 28 years.
Example: The calendar for 2004 will be exactly the same in 2032.
Example: The calendar for 2005 (2004+1) will be the same in 2011.
Example: The calendar for 2006 (2004+2) will be the same in 2017.
